title: TB4-10404
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: This is the decision in the claim of XXXX XXXX XXXX(a.k.a. XXXX XXXX) (the claimant). He purports to be a citizen of China and has applied for refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. He alleges he cannot return to China, where he will be persecuted by the authorities because he is a Tibetan and a follower of the Dalai Lama.

I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee, as he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground in his country of citizenship. Nor is he a person in need of protection as his removal to said country would not subject him personally to a risk to life, to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or to a danger of torture.

The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has intervened on the basis of credibility, alleging that the claimant is a citizen of India, not China, as the claimant entered Canada on an Indian passport, which the Minister believes to be genuine.1

On a balance of probabilities, I do not find the claimant to be a credible witness. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that he is a citizen of India. He has made no allegations that he is at risk of harm or persecution in India.

The claimant is an 18-year-old ethnic Tibetan, born and raised in India. The claimant's grandparents fled from Tibet after the Chinese occupation. The claimant's parents and the claimant himself were born in India. Neither his parents nor he are entitled to citizenship in India. His parents have registered foreign certificates, which allow them to remain in India. The claimant does not have one as he left India around the same time that he was supposed to get one.

The claimant alleges that he cannot obtain citizenship in India and that his status in said country is tenuous. He fears return to his country of citizenship, China, where he will be persecuted because he is Tibetan, an advocate of a Free Tibet and a follower of the Dalai Lama.

I accept that the claimant is named XXXX XXXX XXXXand is known to the Indian authorities by that name. I have evidence of this through his visa application to Canada and the fact that he entered Canada on an Indian passport.2 I accept that he was born in India. I accept, on a balance of probabilities, that he is an ethnic Tibetan. However, I do not accept that the claimant is a citizen of China. Rather, I find him to be citizen of India. The determinative matter at hand is credibility. I do not find the claimant to be a credible witness for the following reasons: The Claimant's Indian Passport, On a Balance of Probabilities, is Genuine

The claimant testified that on XXXX XXXX, 2014, he entered Canada on an Indian passport, which contained his photograph and his date of birth, as well as his signature. He stated that the smuggler hired by his parents required him to sign a blank form. The claimant's name in the passport is XXXX XXXX XXXX.

This above consistent with the passport information and the date of entry as contained within the Minister's information.3 In Schedule 12 (part of the Minister's documents used to determine the claimant's eligibility), the claimant listed all the documents in his possession and those used to travel to Canada. The claimant listed an Indian passport and stated that the document is 'genuine'.4 The claimant testified that this passport was not a legitimate one, as he is not entitled to Indian citizenship. He stated that once he arrived in Canada, he destroyed the Indian passport as per the instructions of the smuggler. I asked the claimant why he stated his Indian passport was genuine in Schedule 12, when in fact it was not. The claimant replied that this was an error. I asked how this error came to be and the claimant replied that he did not know the meaning of the word genuine. The claimant testified that he filled out the forms, together with an interpreter named XXXX, at the interpreter's house. I asked him if he asked the interpreter the meaning of the word 'genuine'. He replied that he did not.

I suggested to him that he did know what the word genuine meant, for he had stated in the same section of Schedule 12 that he was in possession of a genuine Green Book. The claimant replied that it was a mistake; that he simply ticked both boxes saying the documents are genuine without knowing the meaning of the word.

I asked the claimant if he thought the Immigration forms he was completing were important. He replied that he did not think about it. He testified that at the inland Immigration office, he told the interpreter (another interpreter, not XXXX) that his passport was not genuine. I asked the claimant why the error had not been corrected in Schedule 12. He replied that he did not know. The claimant also stated that this interpreter did not go through the forms in detail. I pointed out that he signed Schedule 12 at the end, stating that all the information therein was true, complete and correct. He stated that this was not the case.

I do not believe the claimant's explanation for indicating his Indian passport is genuine, when it is not. The claimant completed his forms after he had retained counsel. He had the assistance of two interpreters to complete the Immigration forms contained in Exhibit 1. He states in his Basis of Claim form5 that he has no right to Indian citizenship and in Schedule 12 that his Green Book is genuine. I note that he was educated in English and that he is a good student; good enough to be enrolled into an English-speaking university (XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX6) to study psychology. I note that the claimant told the panel that his grades were genuine and not fabricated by the agent in order to facilitate admission.

His explanation that his statement that his Indian passport is genuine is a mistake is not a reasonable explanation under the circumstances. I note that while the claimant may be young, he is not unsophisticated. He traveled to Canada, made a refugee claim and retained and instructed counsel with respect to his claim. Ultimately, the claimant and not the interpreter is responsible for the content of his forms.

I believe that the claimant's first answer, that his Indian passport is a genuine one (like his Green Book), on a balance of probabilities, is the truth. This is the reason why this statement was not corrected at the Immigration interview on XXXX XXXX, 2014. The claimant saw no need to make this correction because it was the truth and therefore did not need the correction. The claimant's unreasonable explanation for why he initially stated his Indian passport is genuine (a mistake) detracts from his overall credibility. The Claimant's Expired Green Book

The claimant presented his Green Book in support of his Tibetan identity.7 I note that this document was issued by the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) on XXXX XXXX, 2005 and expired on XXXX XXXX, 2010.8

I asked the claimant why his Green Book was expired. He replied that he did not know. He stated that his parents applied for this book on his behalf. I asked him if the Green Book was used to make financial donations to the government in exile. He replied he did not know. I asked him if he made any donations to the government in exile. He replied that he had not. Furthermore, he was not aware of any financial donation by his parents. I stated that the Green Book allows individuals to vote, to stand for election and to be eligible for CTA scholarships.9 He stated he knew nothing about this.

A Research for Information Request (RIR) from the Immigration and Refugee Board highlight the functions of the Green Book, which is a 'passport' for exiled Tibetans to claim their rights from the CTA. The Green Book is the most official document issued by the CTA and grounds for persecution in China. The CTA states that the "Green Book is designed to serve the purpose of [an] identity certificate [for] Tibetans nationals in lieu of a passport. The holder of the Green Book is recognized as a bonafide Tibetan."10 Once the Green Book is issued (and it can be issued to adults and children), the holder once aged six and above is expected to make voluntary contributions on an annual basis. For example, Tibetans aged six to seventeen years in Canada contribute $36 per year and aged six to fourteen years in India contribute twelve rupees per year.11

The Green Book must be up to date for a Tibetan to exercise his or her rights. Late payments since 2004 or 2005 are associated with a penalty fee.12 I note that the claimant's Green Book has been expired since 2010. I also note that the Green Book does not contain any donations made by the claimant or by his parents.

I want to be clear here. The expired Green Book does not mean that the claimant is not an ethnic Tibetan. I note that the expired Green Book is the claimant's only identity document. He stated he does not have a birth certificate, nor does he have a registered foreigner's certificate as his parents. I asked the claimant how it was that his parents enrolled him in school without documentation. He replied he did know.

The fact that the claimant and his parents allowed his Green Book to expire leads the panel to conclude that the claimant had other documentation to support his identity, namely an Indian passport, the same Indian passport that the claimant initially described as genuine and used to enter Canada. Summary

Based on my analysis above, I make the following findings: * The claimant is an ethnic Tibetan born in India. * I do not find him to be a credible witness with respect to his assertion that the Indian passport used to enter Canada was fraudulent. Rather, I rely on his admission that his Indian passport is a genuine one. * The claimant is no longer a citizen of China, as he has acquired Indian citizenship.13 * The fact that the claimant was a national of India explains why he (and his parents) was not diligent in the renewal of his Green Book. He did not need his Green Book, because he had identity documents that established he was a citizen of India. * Counsel has argued that Tibetans have difficulty in obtaining Indian citizenship though they may be entitled to it by operation of law. But this is not the issue here. The issue is not whether the claimant is entitled to Indian citizenship, but whether he has a genuine Indian passport as he stated in his immigration forms.14 * I find he does and therefore his claim must fail, as he has not raised any reason why he cannot return to India, his country of citizenship.

After a careful review of the evidence before the panel, I find that the claimant is a citizen of India. He is not a citizen of China. He has not alleged a fear of return to India. Therefore, his claim must fail. (signed) "R.K. Seyan" R.K. Seyan "February 23, 2015" Date 1 Exhibit 5. 2 Exhibit 1, GCMS Information Application.
